chapter_theme: A single song at Thanthondri (தான் தோன்றி): the poet asks to understand that this body, a hut propped up by deeds, rots and ends as fine ash, and to be ruled so that, past burning and past deeds, he worships the feet; the praise plays on the shrine's name, the Lord who stands self-arisen.

800.reading: The poet speaks of this hut of a body, a pillar rooted in sorrowful deeds, which tires, wears out, decays and becomes fine ash in the fire, and of not grasping that flaw; like those who dig through learning seeking great wealth and come with outstretched hands, he has gone astray, and asks to be taken as a servant so that, with burning and deeds gone, he worships the good feet in the way that bears fruit. The praise shows ascetics and gods tending his feet, Murugan on the sky-high peacock with arms embraced by his golden-bangled consorts, the vel that fought the Suras of the sunken hill, and the son of the Father of Thanthondri, able to stand self-arisen (தான்தோன்றி).
800.nuance: The song is built of long-vowel clusters ending in -ந்த, -ன்ற (சூழ்ந்தேன்ற, வீழ்ந்தீண்டி, வாழ்ந்தான்ற), so word division is often a guess. The last line puns on the shrine: தான்தோன்றி is both the place and the Lord who appears of himself. வேம் பாங்கும் அற்று வினையாம் பாங்கும் அற்று may mean freedom from burning (birth and death) and from deeds; the simile of the learned beggars is unclear.
